title: Distributed Systems Theory
summary: The moment your system spans two machines, clocks disagree and a dead node looks just like a slow one. These are the proven tools — consensus, clocks, quorums — for taming that chaos.

blocks.markdown:
A distributed system is many computers pretending to be one — over a network that lies.

- The network can **drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder** any message; any node can crash anytime.
- **Three hard truths:** partial failure, no shared clock, unreliable network.
- A **slow node and a dead node look identical** from outside — the root of most pain.
- Everything below — consensus, clocks, quorums — buys correctness against those facts.

blocks.subTitle: Pick the right tool
blocks.markdown:
Match the need to the mechanism — and avoid the wrong one.

| If you need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| One leader / ordered log | Raft or Multi-Paxos |
| Atomic commit across DBs | 2PC (accept blocking) |
| Order events, no synced clock | Lamport / vector clocks |
| Spread state to 1000s of nodes | Gossip |
| Read-your-write on replicas | Quorum (R + W > N) |

blocks.subTitle: Consensus: the keystone
blocks.markdown:
Consensus is getting a group of nodes to agree on one value despite crashes and lost messages.

- **Agreement** — every node that decides picks the same value.
- **Validity** — the value was actually proposed.
- **Termination** — nodes eventually decide.
- Solve it once and you get **leader election, locks, config, and replicated state** — etcd, ZooKeeper, and Consul are all consensus systems.

blocks.subTitle: Raft — consensus you can explain
blocks.markdown:
Raft splits consensus into **leader election** and **log replication**.

- Time is cut into numbered **terms**, each with at most one leader.
- A follower hearing no **heartbeat** before its randomized timeout (150–300 ms) becomes a candidate and asks for votes.
- A candidate winning a **majority** becomes leader and takes all client writes.
- The leader appends each command and replicates via **AppendEntries**.

blocks.subTitle: Why committed data survives
blocks.markdown:
An entry is **committed** once a majority of nodes have it durably — not all of them.

- Any two majorities of N nodes **overlap by at least one node**.
- A node only votes for a candidate whose log is **at least as up-to-date** as its own.
- So any majority that can elect a leader must contain every committed entry — the new leader never loses committed data.
- This overlap trick is the whole reason quorums work.

blocks.subTitle: Trace a Raft write
blocks.markdown:
One client write through a 3-node cluster — commit needs a majority ack, not all.

```text
1. Client -> N1 (leader): write(x=42)
2. N1 appends index=58, term=4   (uncommitted)
3. N1 -> AppendEntries to N2, N3 in parallel
4. N2 log matches up to 57? yes -> fsync, ACK
5. N1 + N2 = 2 of 3 = MAJORITY -> COMMIT, apply
6. N1 -> Client: OK
```

- Step 5 is the beat: a slow or dead N3 doesn't block the write.
- Cost is **one round trip to the faster follower + an fsync** (~2 ms same-region).

blocks.subTitle: FLP — you can't have it all
blocks.markdown:
FLP proves no deterministic algorithm can **always** reach consensus in a purely asynchronous network where one node may crash.

- You can't tell a crashed node from an infinitely slow one, so an adversary can delay the deciding message forever.
- It's a precise trade-off, not a doomsday verdict.
- Real systems add **timeouts** (a weak failure detector): keep **safety always**, accept the system may **stall** during a bad partition.
- That stall is the price FLP says you must pay somewhere.

blocks.subTitle: Logical clocks
blocks.markdown:
Wall clocks lie, so order events by **causality**: if A could have caused B, A comes first.

- **Lamport clock** — one counter per node; on receive, set `counter = max(local, t) + 1`. Guarantees A→B implies LC(A) < LC(B), but **can't detect concurrency**.
- **Vector clock** — one counter slot per node; on receive, take element-wise max then bump your slot.
- If neither vector dominates, the events are **concurrent** — exactly the conflict signal Dynamo-style stores use.

blocks.subTitle: Gossip & quorums
blocks.markdown:
Two ways big clusters coordinate without a central boss.

- **Gossip** — each node periodically tells a few random peers what it knows; info reaches all N in about **O(log N) rounds**. No single point of failure, scales hugely, but only **eventually consistent**.
- **Quorum** — require W replicas to ack a write and R to answer a read. If **R + W > N**, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so reads see the newest value.
- Common pick: N=3, W=2, R=2.

blocks.subTitle: The big levers
blocks.markdown:
Every distributed choice trades one good thing for another.

- **Consistency vs availability under partition (CAP)** — refuse requests to stay consistent (CP) or keep serving and reconcile later (AP). You can't have both *during* a partition.
- **Latency vs safety** — waiting for a majority is durable but adds a round trip; acking after one node is fast but loses data on failover.
- **Order vs scale** — a single leader gives clean total order but caps write throughput; gossip scales but is only eventual.

blocks.subTitle: Rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Reach for the proven, simple tool first.

- **Single source of truth** (leader, lock, config) → a consensus system; don't roll your own.
- **Atomic commit, one trust domain, brief blocking OK** → 2PC; otherwise sagas or consensus-backed commit ([b08-consistency-replication](b08-consistency-replication.md)).
- **Order without synced clocks** → Lamport for order, vector clocks to *detect* concurrency.
- **Thousands of nodes, eventual agreement** → gossip.
- **Always size clusters odd (3/5/7)** and keep them small.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The theory shows up directly in systems you depend on.

- **etcd / Kubernetes** — Raft-backed key-value store, the brain of K8s; CP, so the minority side of a partition can't make changes. Run 3 or 5, never even.
- **Google Spanner** — Paxos per shard, **2PC over Paxos** so the coordinator is fault-tolerant; **TrueTime** waits out clock uncertainty before committing.
- **DynamoDB / Cassandra** — AP: leaderless, tunable quorums, gossip for membership, vector clocks to detect concurrent writes.
- **ZooKeeper** — Zab consensus; ephemeral znodes make clean lock primitives.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Timestamps order my events."** Clocks disagree and drift — use logical clocks, not wall-clock time.
- **"No response means it failed."** A timeout tells you nothing; the work may have succeeded. Make mutations **idempotent**.
- **"More nodes make consensus faster."** Throughput is capped by the leader and the majority wait; more voters add latency.
- **"2PC gives free distributed transactions."** It **blocks** when the coordinator dies mid-flight, holding locks.
- **"A majority quorum always gives fresh reads."** Only if reads go through the quorum or leader — random followers return stale data.
